lessons.title: A Decision Framework: Matching Property Type to Your Capital, Goals and Temperament

children.text: By now you can calculate net yield, value a pre-leased unit, model IRR and read a lease. Yet two people with identical spreadsheets can still make opposite decisions and both be right. A 30-year-old saving for a home, a 50-year-old HNI seeking income and a 66-year-old retiree face the same property market with completely different lives. This lesson turns everything in the course into a decision framework: five filters that match residential, commercial or indirect routes such as REITs to your capital, goals and temperament.

body.text: There is no best property type, only the best fit. Start with your life, not the listing: your capital, your goal, your horizon, your need for cash and how much effort and uncertainty you can handle.

This framework is educational and general. It is not personalised investment advice. For decisions about your own money, speak with a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a qualified tax professional.

markDefs.definition: A check of whether a single investment is so large relative to your net worth that one bad outcome, such as a price fall or a year of vacancy, would derail your finances.

children.text: Start with how much you can invest without putting your financial plan at risk. Keep your emergency fund and near-term goals separate first. Then run the
: if this single property fell 30% in value or earned nothing for a year, would your plans survive?

body.label: The one-bad-year test
body.value: Could you absorb a year with no rent?
body.context: If losing one year of income from this property would force you to sell, borrow expensively or cut essential spending, the investment is too concentrated for direct ownership. Consider a smaller ticket or an indirect route.

children.text: Capital also decides what is realistically on the menu. Under about ₹10 lakh, listed REITs are the practical route to commercial property. From ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh, SM REITs, a small residential unit in a tier-2 city or a diversified REIT portfolio come into view. Direct commercial units with decent tenants usually start around ₹50 lakh and above, and diversifying across several needs crores.

body.text: The home you live in is a different decision from investment property. It buys security, stability and control over where your family lives, benefits that never appear in an IRR. Judge a home to live in partly on life needs, and judge investment property strictly on numbers.

children.text: Filter 3: Horizon and the Cost of Getting In and Out

markDefs.definition: The total cost of buying and later selling an asset, such as stamp duty, registration, legal fees and brokerage. For Indian property, commonly around 8% to 10% of value.

children.text: : around 7% for stamp duty and registration on entry and 1% to 2% brokerage on exit. Spread over a short holding period, those costs overwhelm any yield advantage.

body.caption: A rough guide that ignores compounding; it shows why short holding periods punish direct property.

body.title: Approximate annual cost drag from 9% round-trip costs

children.text: A 3-year hold loses about 3% a year to costs, which can wipe out a residential yield entirely. Beyond 7 to 10 years, the drag falls below about 1.3% a year. If your horizon is under 5 years, listed REITs, which trade with normal brokerage and no stamp duty on purchase, are usually the more sensible property exposure.

Ask two questions. First, might you need this money back at short notice? If yes, direct property of any kind is a poor fit, and listed REITs are the only property route with real liquidity. Second, if you borrow, who pays the EMI? With Indian residential yields well below home loan rates, your salary carries the loan. With a strong pre-leased commercial unit, the rent can largely carry it. If your income is uncertain or seasonal, avoid borrowing structures that depend on it.

body.title: Which will you be happier living with?

columns.label: You may suit direct residential if you
points: Can handle frequent small tenant tasks
Are comfortable with low income for years
Believe strongly in a specific neighbourhood
Have a long horizon and a stable salary

columns.label: You may suit direct commercial if you
points: Want strong income and can read leases
Can tolerate rare but large vacancy shocks
Have enough capital to keep a vacancy reserve
Can evaluate a business tenant's finances

children.text: If neither column describes you, because you want property exposure without tenants, paperwork or large single bets, and you can accept daily price movements, listed REITs are likely the better fit. Many investors end up combining routes: a home to live in, plus REITs for commercial income.

body.text: Do not let a single factor make the decision for you. A tax exemption, a relative's advice, a "last few units left" offer or a single year of strong price growth are all poor reasons to buy. Run all five filters every time.

body.title: Calculate: A Weighted Decision Score
body.prompt: A retiree weights her priorities as Income now 30%, Liquidity 25%, Low effort 20% and Long-term growth 25%. She scores a direct flat as Income 1, Liquidity 2, Low effort 2, Growth 4 (total 2.20) and listed REITs as 4, 5, 5, 3 (total 4.20). A pre-leased office scores Income 5, Liquidity 2, Low effort 3, Growth 3. What is the office's weighted score? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 0.30 × 5 + 0.25 × 2 + 0.20 × 3 + 0.25 × 3 = 1.50 + 0.50 + 0.60 + 0.75 = 3.35. For her priorities, the office beats the flat but trails listed REITs, mainly on liquidity and effort. A different investor with different weights could reach the opposite ranking.

body.title: Quick Check: The Short Horizon
body.question: Rohan expects to need his ₹40 lakh back in about 3 years for a business expansion. He wants property exposure meanwhile. Which route best fits the framework?
options: A residential flat, because prices usually rise
A pre-leased shop, because its yield is higher
Listed REITs, because they avoid heavy round-trip costs and can be sold quickly
A plot in a growth corridor, because it has no maintenance
body.explanation: With a 3-year horizon, round-trip costs of about 9% on direct property would drag returns by roughly 3% a year, and he may not be able to sell in time. Listed REITs avoid stamp duty on purchase and trade daily, though their prices can fall in the short term.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Getting In and Out
body.textWithBlank: The total of stamp duty, registration, legal fees and brokerage to buy and later sell a property is called its round-___ cost.
body.explanation: Round-trip costs of around 8% to 10% make direct property a poor fit for short holding periods.

body.title: Scenario: A Couple Who Disagree
body.scenario: Aditya and Sneha, both 42, live in Pune with two children aged 10 and 7. They have ₹90 lakh to invest after keeping an emergency fund. Aditya, a bank manager with a stable salary, wants a second flat in Hinjewadi because "property is safe and the kids can have it later". Sneha, a freelance designer with irregular income, wants monthly income and hates the idea of chasing tenants. The children's college costs begin in about 8 years.
body.prompt: Run the five filters and suggest a direction that respects both of them.
body.modelAnswer: Capital: ₹90 lakh is enough for one direct property but not several, so any single asset is concentrated. Goal: they share two goals, college costs in about 8 years and some long-term wealth for the children, plus Sneha's wish for income. Horizon: 8 years softens round-trip costs to about 1.1% a year, so direct property is viable, but they must be able to sell or raise cash around year 8. Liquidity and leverage: college needs make liquidity important, and Sneha's irregular income argues against a loan that depends on salary. Temperament: Aditya values tangible ownership; Sneha values income and low effort. A reasonable direction is a split. For example, part of the money in a ready flat bought without a loan to satisfy Aditya's long-term ownership goal, and part in listed REITs for Sneha's income and to provide liquidity for college. A single pre-leased commercial unit could meet the income goal but puts too much on one tenant for a family with fixed college deadlines. They should discuss exact proportions with a SEBI-registered investment adviser.

body.title: Your Property Decision Worksheet
steps: Capital: how much can I invest after my emergency fund and near-term goals?
Concentration: could I survive this property falling 30% or earning nothing for a year?
Goal: is this money for income, growth, a future home or flexibility?
Horizon: will I hold for at least 7 to 10 years, or do I need a lower-cost route?
Liquidity: might I need this money back suddenly?
Leverage: if I borrow, will rent or my salary carry the EMI?
Temperament: how much effort, control and price volatility do I want?
Tax: how will rent and eventual sale be taxed for me?
Decision: which route passes all filters, and what is my realistic bad case?

cards.definition: Checking whether one property is so large that a single bad outcome would derail your finances.
All costs to buy and later sell a property, commonly around 8% to 10% in India.
Round-trip costs spread over the holding period, reducing the annual return.
The likelihood that you will need the invested money back at short notice.
Whether rent or your own income pays the costs and EMI of holding a property.
A way to compare options by rating them on criteria weighted by your own priorities.

points: Match property to your life using five filters: capital, goal, horizon, liquidity and leverage, and temperament.
Run the concentration test: if one year without rent or a 30% fall would derail you, the bet is too big for direct ownership.
Round-trip costs of around 9% make direct property a poor fit for holding periods under about 5 years.
Income goals favour strong pre-leased commercial property or REITs; growth and future-home goals favour residential.
If liquidity matters or you want low effort, listed REITs are usually the best-fitting property route.
Combining routes, such as a home to live in plus REITs for income, often fits real lives better than a single choice.
